abstract: This study analyzes how generative AI adoption by firms changes labor demand across different worker groups using a sample of 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records across 41 countries. The authors develop a model decomposing employment changes into firm-wide productivity effects and worker-type-specific task content changes, then estimate effects via an instrumented event study comparing foreign affiliates of AI-adopting companies to control affiliates. Results show AI adoption primarily shifts employment toward senior workers in AI-exposed occupations while reducing junior employment demand, with modest overall employment growth of 3.3 percent and evidence of productivity gains that are seniority-biased.
keyFindings: Senior employment at treated affiliates rises by 6.7 percent while junior employment declines by 2.5 percent (not statistically significant), resulting in a 1.9 percentage point decrease in junior employment share by March 2026.
Total employment grows by a marginally significant 3.3 percent at AI-adopting affiliates, indicating the scale effect of productivity gains offsets labor-saving effects for most worker groups.

Senior workers shift toward AI-exposed occupations (5 percent increase), while junior workers shift away from these occupations (2 percent decrease), with computer and mathematical occupations showing the largest seniority bias (junior share falls 3.3 points).

The decline in junior employment share appears across 23 of 31 countries studied, with statistically significant declines in the United States, Brazil, and Saudi Arabia, showing geographically widespread effects.

AI adoption is identified as labor-saving for junior workers and labor-expanding for seniors in exposed occupations, with model-based decomposition suggesting modest seniority-biased productivity gains from AI.
methodology: Event study design using 1.25 billion job postings and 154 million employment records from Revelio Labs across 41 countries from January 2021 through March 2026. AI adoption measured from job postings involving generative AI (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) using LLM-based screening. Sample includes 395,638 affiliates overall, with 100,813 foreign affiliates in estimation sample. Identification strategy uses two steps: (1) matching treated affiliates to observably similar control affiliates in same country and sector; (2) instrumenting for company-level AI adoption using adoption rate among peer multinational parents headquartered in same metropolitan area. Monthly affiliate-level panel tracks employment size and composition by occupation (22 groups) and seniority level. Treatment dated at November 2022 (ChatGPT launch) for all treated affiliates. Analysis decomposes employment changes into scale effects (identified from unexposed occupations) and type-specific labor demand shifters.
qualifiers: Results apply to digitally-attached multinational firms with LinkedIn presence; composition of such firms may vary across countries affecting cross-country comparisons. LinkedIn data shows non-representative occupational coverage: roughly two-thirds of U.S. employment, one-quarter in Brazil and Germany, only 8 percent in India, with oversampling of managers and professionals. Revelio employment grows faster than official employment, likely from platform growth rather than participation changes. U.S. posting data ends October 2025, missing late adopters. Identification requires that peer adoption around parent headquarters affects affiliate workforce only through multinational's own AI adoption; pre-trends and robustness checks support this assumption. Point estimates for junior employment declines (2.5 percent) not statistically significant. Author notes that general equilibrium effects may differ from firm-level adopter-control comparisons due to wage, price, and labor supply feedback. AI posting data screening vocabulary uses English terms though model and product names used internationally; some non-English-speaking countries have higher AI-posting shares than English-speaking ones suggesting limited systematic bias.
